name: PT Samudera Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Samudera Indonesia — a cash-generative carrier priced for a permanent freight winter
frontmatter.summary: Samudera Indonesia carries Indonesian and regional trade at half of book and five times earnings, yet its nine-month revenue is up double digits and the fleet is being expanded into a market where demand exceeds tonnage. We initiate at BUY; the price implies flat-to-falling revenue forever.
thesis: The market capitalises group EBIT at a mid-single-digit multiple even though the carrier has been earning a double-digit operating margin for three straight years and generated over one hundred million dollars of operating cash flow before capex in the last twelve months.
Revenue growth is already booked, not hoped for; the first nine months of 2026 grew more than a tenth with tariffs still rising into 2027, and management guides to matching the prior record year.
The nine-vessel newbuild programme lands in 2027-28 into a market where the chief executive says demand already exceeds available capacity; growth capex is in our numbers, not bolted on afterwards.

A balance sheet at effectively zero net debt, a dividend at a mid-single-digit yield and close to four-fifths insider ownership mean the equity is not dependent on refinancing or on a rights issue to fund the fleet.
The discount is real but it is a discount for illiquidity and family control, not for a broken business; those are the two facts a buyer has to accept, and both are quantified in this note.

catalysts.event: Full-year 2026 results; fourth-quarter tariff realisation and the first guidance for 2027
Annual general meeting and final dividend decision for the 2026 book year
Delivery and deployment of the newbuild container ships and chemical tankers ordered in 2026
October-November trade prints from the statistics agency, the read-across to container volumes

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Samudera Indonesia with a **BUY** rating and a twelve-month target of Rp870, against a last price of Rp320: an expected total return of 175.9% including the dividend. That is an uncomfortable distance from the market price, and most of this note is about why we think it is the market that is wrong rather than the model.

The business earned revenue of 801.7 in FY2025 and an operating profit of 91.6 [S0][S3]. In the first nine months of 2026 revenue grew to 647 USD m with gross profit of 114 USD m, G&A of 38.4 USD m and an operating profit of 75.4 USD m [S5][S2]. Reported EBITDA was 205 USD m in that period against 200 USD m for the whole of FY2025 [S2][S3]. Net profit attributable to shareholders was 50.9 USD m for the nine months, up eighteen percent, on finance costs of 23.6 USD m and interest income of 10.4 USD m [S5].

At today's price the shares trade on 5.6x trailing earnings, 0.5x book and 3.8% dividend yield [S0]. At 30 September 2026 the group carried net debt of 2.5 USD m, after cash of 342 USD m and short-term investments of 169 USD m against total debt of 513 USD m [S17]; the FY2026E model line carries net debt of -14.8, a net cash position, or -0.1 times EBITDA [S0], and the two are labelled separately. A carrier at effectively zero net debt, with positive free cash flow and a fleet being expanded, does not normally trade at half of book unless the market believes the earnings are a cycle peak. Our view is that the earnings are not a peak: the operating margin has been 91.6 on 801.7 of revenue in the last full year, within a whisker of the two years before it, and the driver of the next two years is not a freight spike but additional ships [S7].

Three things move the value. First, the tariff line: management says freight rates are already above the second half of 2025 and that demand exceeds the fleet it can deploy [S10]. Second, the capital intensity of the newbuild programme, which we charge in full from FY2027E at 21.0% of revenue, so the target does not depend on under-spending on the fleet [S7]. Third, the discount rate: this is a micro-cap with a free float of 19.2% and a three-month traded value of IDR11.5bn a day [S0], and we discount it at 13.5% rather than at the bottom of the house band.

What today's price implies is worth stating plainly. Our reverse DCF says the market is discounting revenue growth of -1.8% from 2027 onwards, against the 7.5% we forecast [S0][S7]. In other words the shares are priced for a permanent contraction in the freight market rather than for a cycle. If that is what happens, the bear case priced at Rp349 is the one that matters — and even that case sits above the current price. We would rather own the base case.

Samudera Indonesia is an Indonesian shipping and logistics group listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange and controlled by PT Samudera Indonesia Tangguh, which holds the great majority of the shares; the free float is 19.2% and insiders hold 77.8% [S0]. The group was founded in the nineteen sixties and is headquartered in Jakarta, with 5,229 employees [S0]. It reports in US dollars, which matters for how the shares should be valued: the revenue line is a dollar line even though the equity is quoted in rupiah.

The company operates through three reported segments — shipping and agency, logistics and ports, and other services [S0]. Shipping is the core. It runs liner and feeder container services, a fleet that includes bulk carriers, LNG and gas carriers and chemical tankers, offshore support and salvage work, bunker supply and project shipping for the oil and gas industry; the group also provides crew and ship management, agency services, ship repair and fabrication [S0]. The logistics and ports arm operates terminals and hinterland logistics, and management is explicit that the Patimban port business is part of the expansion story [S7].

The operating footprint is the thing to understand about the franchise. By the third quarter of 2026 the shipping network reached 28.0 countries countries and called at ports across the region, according to the company [S5]. That is a regional rather than a global network, built around Indonesian domestic trades, intra-Asia container routes and a growing Indian and Middle Eastern presence [S0]. For an Indonesian exporter or importer, the value of the network is that it connects a domestic leg to an international one on a single through bill; that is a distribution-density moat rather than a cost moat.

The Indonesian liner market has three structural features that shape every operator. Cabotage rules reserve
domestic sea carriage to nationally flagged vessels, which keeps foreign lines out of the archipelago's
inter-island trade. The trade itself is lopsided: a handful of routes carry most container volume, and the
eastern islands are served at high cost and low frequency. And the state-owned line is the residual carrier
of last resort on thin routes, so private operators compete on the dense western corridors and on
international connecting services rather than on universal coverage.

Growth is being bought with steel. At the end of October 2026 the company had signed contracts for 5.0 vessels new vessels — three container ships and two chemical tankers being built in China — and was finalising four more, for delivery from 2027 into 2028 [S7]. The chief executive framed the order book against a market in which demand for capacity already exceeds the fleet available to serve it [S7][S8].

The group also holds non-controlled interests, and the size of the minority line is a permanent feature of the equity story: minorities took 27.0 of FY2025 net profit [S0]. Any valuation has to deduct the minority stake, which we do at book value in the bridge.

The industry SMDR sells into is the carriage of Indonesian and intra-Asian trade, in containers, dry bulk, liquid chemicals and gas [S0][S5]. Its revenue is a direct function of three variables: the volume of cargo moved, the freight rate per unit and the utilisation of the fleet it can deploy. Everything else — bunker prices, charter-in rates, port productivity — is a cost pass-through that determines the margin on that revenue.

The volume backdrop in 2026 is strong. Indonesian imports for January to September were 211 USD bn, up almost a fifth on the prior year, driven by raw materials and intermediate goods [S11]; exports over the same period reached a record value, with the processed and agricultural complex doing the heavy lifting [S12]. Containerised imports are the single most relevant series for a liner operator, and the import number is the one that has been accelerating.

The tariff side is where the operating leverage sits. Management told the FY2025 results call that freight rates had begun to rise compared with the second half of 2025 and that this would feed directly into revenue [S10]. By the third quarter of 2026, revenue had grown to 647 USD m against the comparable period, but cost of services grew faster at 534 USD m, so gross profit rose only to 114 USD m [S5]. That gap is the honest picture of the industry in 2026: volumes and rates are good, but bunker and charter-in costs are eating most of the increment. The chief executive said as much, noting that the fuel increase was being passed through to customers without damaging load factors [S8].

Container shipping is a structurally fragmented industry with a consolidated top tier. Globally, a handful
of alliances control most mainline capacity, but the intra-Asia and domestic Indonesian trades are served by
a long tail of regional operators, which is why freight rates on those routes behave more like a spot
market than like an oligopoly price. The economics are brutally simple: a ship is a fixed cost once it
sails, so utilisation is everything, and a two-point swing in load factor moves the operating margin more
than a ten percent move in the fuel price. Newbuilding decisions are made years ahead of delivery, which
guarantees that capacity arrives exactly when the cycle has turned.

Regulation cuts both ways. Cabotage protection gives Indonesian-flagged operators a captive domestic market and a cost advantage over foreign lines that cannot serve inter-island legs; the flip side is that the domestic fleet is old, and renewal is expensive. The tax regime is the most valuable single feature of the sector for shareholders: Indonesian shipping income is taxed on a deemed basis rather than at the headline corporate rate, and the accounts bear this out — the effective charge has been in the high single digits as a percentage of pre-tax profit [S0].

On competition, SMDR is a leading domestic challenger rather than the incumbent: the state line is larger on subsidised routes, and several private groups compete on the dense Java-Sumatra and Java-Sulawesi corridors. SMDR's differentiation is the combination of an international network and a domestic feeder system, plus terminal access at Patimban [S7]. Our five-forces read is: supplier power moderate (shipyards and charter markets are cyclical, and there is a live order book), buyer power high (shippers can and do switch on price for commodity cargo), threat of new entry low domestically because of cabotage and capital, threat of substitutes low for island trade, and rivalry high but rational on the dense routes.

The moat, then, is density and route rights rather than brand or switching costs [S7][S5]. That supports a durable business but not pricing power, which is exactly why we value it on cash flow with an explicit fade rather than on a growth multiple.

Revenue peaked in FY2022 at 1,151.0 on the post-pandemic freight spike, fell to 772.4 as rates normalised, and has since rebuilt to 801.7 [S0][S3]. The operating margin told the same story: 341.1 of EBIT in FY2022, then 104.7, 95.1 and 91.6 [S0]. What matters for the forecast is that the last three years have been remarkably stable at a double-digit margin on a much larger revenue base — this is not a company earning spike profits.

**The D&A restatement is the most important adjustment in this model, and it is a P&L charge, not a cash-flow plug.** The data pack's depreciation line for FY2025 is a fraction of the real charge, which is impossible for a group with a fleet: it is an artefact of the direct-method cash-flow statement Indonesian issuers file, and we discard it. The reported cash-flow statement shows depreciation and amortisation of 98.9 USD m in FY2025 and 76.1 USD m in FY2024 [S16]. We do not take that historical ratio forward on faith. The nine-month 2026 accounts fix the current run-rate: EBITDA of 205 USD m less operating profit of 75.4 USD m over nine-month revenue of 647 USD m is a charge of 17.7% of revenue [S2][S5], higher than FY2025 because vessels and leases were added in 2026. We forecast that rate, and the engine rebuilds EBITDA and free cash flow from it. The reconciliation to the company's own numbers is explicit: our restated FY2025 EBITDA is 190.6 against the company's 200 USD m [S3], the difference being other operating income the company adds back and we leave in EBIT; and capex is held at or above the restated charge in every year, so the higher D&A does not hand free cash flow a fictitious add-back.

Margins: gross profit was 147.3 on 801.7 in FY2025 [S0], and 114 USD m on 647 USD m in the first nine months of 2026, a shade under eighteen percent [S5]. We hold 17.6% for FY2026E and let it recover to 18.6% as tariffs firm, which is the direction management describes [S10]. G&A has been running at 38.4 USD m in the nine months, or close to six percent of revenue, and we hold 6.0% [S5].

Revenue: the nine-month run-rate gets FY2026E to 889.9, growth of 11.0% [S5]. That leaves a fourth quarter of ordinary seasonality. FY2026E parent profit of 51.6 looks close to the nine-month actual of 50.9 USD m, but the comparison is not like for like: the nine months carry 8.2 USD m of foreign-exchange gain and 4.8 USD m of asset-sale gains [S5], neither of which our forecast repeats. Strip them and the implied fourth quarter is up on the fourth quarter of 2025, not down — there is no earnings cliff, and the nine-month EBITDA margin of the reported accounts is reproduced by the full-year forecast. We then grow 7.5% in FY2027E and 7.0% in FY2028E as the nine-vessel programme delivers — all nine, not only the five under contract, so the capex charged for them is matched by revenue — fading to 4.5% and 3.5% as the order book is absorbed [S7]. That gives EBIT of 103.2 rising to 137.3.

Cash flow and capex: capex was 81.7 in FY2025, about a tenth of revenue [S0]. We deliberately run it above that — 18.5% of revenue in FY2026E, peaking at 21.0% in FY2027E and FY2028E — because nine vessels cost money and because a fleet must be renewed at replacement cost, not at historic cost [S7]. Free cash flow to the firm is 97.0 in FY2026E, dips during the delivery years, and recovers thereafter; it is the dip that makes the target credible rather than heroic.
Working capital is small and fast: operating working capital has run between one and four percent of revenue [S0], and we assume 2.0% — shippers pay quickly and the group is not financing inventory.

Balance sheet: at the end of September 2026 total assets were 1,500 USD m and equity, including minority interests, was 808 USD m [S2]. The liquid position is a composition question and we state it in full: cash and cash equivalents of 342 USD m plus short-term investments of 169 USD m, which are time deposits and marketable securities rather than restricted cash [S17]. Total debt is 513 USD m, of which lease liabilities are the larger part [S17]. Net debt at that date was 2.5 USD m [S17] — on the balance-sheet date the group is marginally geared, not net cash. That is a different measure from the -14.8 our model carries for FY2026E, which is a forecast year-end line and assumes the fourth quarter's free cash flow turns the position to net cash; the two are not one balance sheet and we do not present them as one. Minority interests at the same date were 235 USD m [S17]. Interest cover on EBITDA of 260.7 against interest of 29.6 is comfortable. The finance cost has been creeping up — 23.6 USD m in the nine months against 10.4 USD m of interest income [S5] — but not at a pace that threatens the dividend.

Capital allocation is conservative: the FY2025 dividend of 196 IDR bn, equal to twelve rupiah a share, was approved at the June 2026 meeting [S13], a payout of roughly 21.0% of attributable profit, with the rest retained for the fleet. On our numbers the payout is covered by free cash flow in every forecast year.

Earnings quality. The accruals picture is clean: free cash flow to the firm of 91.8 against net profit of 79.1 and depreciation of 98.9 USD m leaves no gap for a reader to worry about [S0][S16]. Receivables have not outgrown revenue. Two items need naming rather than burying. First, the nine-month profit carries 8.2 USD m of foreign-exchange gain and 4.8 USD m of asset-sale gains [S5]; we strip both from the base and the forecast carries neither, which is why the full-year number sits close to the reported nine months. Second, the structural flags: a minority interest of 235 USD m at the last balance sheet that takes roughly a third of profit, and an effective tax rate that depends on the deemed shipping regime [S17]. Both are disclosed and both are in our model. On related parties, the record we archived shows one affiliate transaction — the December 2022 purchase of a further quarter of LNG East-West Shipping, taking the group to half [S14] — four years before this balance sheet and not a trading flow. We could not quantify related-party sales or purchases as a share of revenue from the archive, and we report that as a gap rather than estimate it.

We value SMDR on a discounted free cash flow to the firm, weighted 55% against a peer P/E cross-check at 35%. The method fits the industry: the assets are long-lived, the cash flows are contracted voyage by voyage but the fleet is a fixed capital base, and earnings are distorted by a depreciation charge that is large relative to profit. A DCF on cash flow after full fleet capex is the right lens; a book-value approach would say little, because an old vessel's book value is not its earning power.

The discount rate comes out at 13.5%, and the build is worth setting out in full because it is not a textbook one. The risk-free rate of 5.1% is the deck's dollar series, which is the right base for a dollar revenue line rather than the rupiah rate. The mature-market equity risk premium is 4.2%, the Indonesian country premium 2.5%, and the unlevered beta 1.25, above the generic industrial default because group EBIT fell by more than two thirds in FY2023 off the pandemic freight peak; it did not fall again in FY2025, when EBIT moved a few percent lower on higher revenue [S0]. The engine then levers that beta at the balance-sheet net debt of 2.5 USD m [S17] against a market capitalisation far below our value, which gives a D/E of 0.01 and a levered beta of 1.26; the cost of equity is 13.5%. The weights are 99.2% equity and 0.8% debt, the pre-tax cost of debt is 7.1%, and after the 22.0% tax charge the WACC is 13.5%. The twelve-month roll that turns the blended value of Rp692 into the base of Rp773 applies that same 13.5% cost of equity.

**The gearing is net, not gross, and the choice moves the answer in the direction that is not obvious.** At 30 September 2026 gross debt of 513 USD m was almost entirely offset by cash of 342 USD m and short-term investments of 169 USD m, leaving net debt of 2.5 USD m [S17]. The owner of this equity is exposed to that net position, not to the gross borrowing, so the beta is re-levered at net debt: the D/E is 0.01, the levered beta 1.26 and the cost of equity 13.5%. The earlier draft levered the same unlevered beta at gross debt against a market capitalisation that is a fraction of our equity value, which printed a cost of equity in the mid-twenties — the rate a highly indebted equity should carry, not a company whose net debt is -0.1 times EBITDA.

The consequence cuts against the intuitive reading, and we state it rather than bury it: in this engine the cost of equity also enters the WACC through the debt weight, and at net gearing that weight collapses to 0.8%. The cheaper cost of equity is more than offset by the loss of the debt weight, so the WACC *rises* to 13.5% relative to a gross-debt build, and the DCF falls rather than rises. That is the correct sign: a company with no net leverage earns no meaningful interest tax shield, and its assets should be discounted at close to the unlevered cost of capital. The same rate compounds the blended value of Rp692 into the base case of Rp773, and the published target of Rp870 is built on this net-gearing cost of capital throughout — model, roll and prose are one convention [S17].

The DCF gives Rp761 a share, with terminal value at 40.0% of the total. The forecast is deliberately unheroic in the back half: revenue growth fades to a low single digit by FY2030E and capex stays at 19.5% of revenue, above depreciation, so the terminal value is not being fed by an under-investment assumption.

The P/E cross-check gives Rp465 on a peer median of 8.1 times earnings — -38.9% against the DCF. The peer set is BIRD, CASS, ELPI, GMFI and TMAS, the five Indonesian transport and logistics names in the pack, and the median is struck across all five: ELPI is the high outlier on a depressed earnings base and BIRD the low one, with CASS the middle name [S0]. The house comps screen, taken on a different date, gives a slightly lower median for the same five names; a five-name median moves with the screen date and neither figure is wrong. We do not average the gap to the DCF away silently. The difference exists because the peer set trades on trailing earnings that the market expects to fall, while our DCF assumes the current operating margin persists and the fleet grows. That is the whole bet. Three observations support our side. The margin has been stable for three years, not one [S0]. The nine-month result is up year on year on higher volumes and higher tariffs, not on a one-off [S5][S10]. And the group's own chief executive says demand exceeds available tonnage, which is not the language of a company at the top of a cycle [S7][S8].

The P/BV cross-check is the one leg that sits above the DCF: it gives Rp1,108 a share, 45.5% against the primary method. That is what a justified book value looks like for a carrier earning close to its cost of equity on a fleet carried near historic cost — the asset base is understated relative to replacement value, so book is a floor rather than a ceiling. It takes the smallest weight for a reason that cuts both ways: a floor is not a forecast. It is precisely because we do not believe the cycle will be kind that we will not let a static book multiple carry the target; but it is also why the bear case still sits above the current price, which is the single most important observation in this note.

The multiple-survival test is the strongest argument against us, and we state it plainly. At the target the shares would trade on a premium to book and a mid-teens multiple of forward earnings, against 5.6x and 0.5x today [S0]. A buyer at that price would be paying for the re-rating, not just for the cash flow. That is why the target is a blend and why the P/E leg carries 35% of the weight rather than a token amount.

Sensitivity is concentrated where you would expect: the gross margin and the discount rate. A one percentage-point change in gross margin moves the DCF value by materially more than a one-point change in the growth rate, because the margin applies to the whole revenue base while growth compounds slowly at these rates.

What the price implies: -1.8% revenue growth from 2027, against the 7.5% we forecast [S0][S7]. Equivalently, the market is paying 0.5x of book for a business earning 9.8% on equity [S0]. Either investors expect that return to halve, or they require a return on this stock far above the cost of capital implied by its beta. Both are defensible; neither is what the last three years of accounts show.

The three cases shock the same four drivers by the same amounts in opposite directions: revenue growth, gross margin, the newbuild capex ratio and net borrowing. The bull takes gross margin to a level still below the FY2023 trough of 21.7% and far below the pandemic peak, so it does not assume a return to spike freight; the bear takes it to a rate-war level and keeps the committed capex with a cost overrun, borrowing the gap at the current cost of debt. The weights are a half to the base and a quarter to each tail. The reader should do the table's arithmetic: each case contributes its probability (0.25, 0.50, 0.25) times its value (Rp349, Rp773, Rp1,584). Because value is convex in the margin, the bull's contribution exceeds the base's at equal weight; the bull is capped at the last cycle's margin for exactly that reason, and the base still carries the largest single weight. The published target is the weighted total of Rp870, against a base-case roll of Rp773 — the weighting is the most likely path, not a tilt.

**Freight cycle (high likelihood, high impact).** The central risk. A liner operator's margin is a residual between a spot-linked tariff and a fixed fleet cost. The right way to size it is the last downturn, not a sentiment haircut: between FY2022 and FY2023 revenue fell to 772.4 from 1,151.0 and EBIT to 104.7 from 341.1, and the bulk of that was gross margin collapsing from 34.2% to 21.7% as the pandemic freight spike unwound [S0]. There is no spike to unwind now — the current gross margin of 18.4% is already below that FY2023 trough — so the bear does not need a second margin collapse of the same size, and we do not pretend one is coming. It cuts gross margin hard from a lower starting point, takes revenue growth lower, keeps the committed newbuild capex with a cost overrun on it, and borrows the funding gap at the current cost of debt [S7][S13]. That produces an EBIT drawdown of the same order as FY2023 and values the shares at Rp349 against Rp320. The bear is a bear; it is simply still above the price, because the market capitalises the equity below book.

**Fuel and charter-in costs (high likelihood, medium impact).** Bunker prices rose through 2026 and cost of services grew faster than revenue in the nine months [S5]. Management says the increase can be passed through [S8]; if it cannot, the margin takes the hit rather than the customer.

**Newbuild execution and funding (medium likelihood, medium impact).** Nine vessels is a large order book relative to the balance sheet. Delivery delays push revenue out; cost overruns and pre-delivery payments consume cash precisely when the dividend is also being paid [S7]. In the base the programme is funded from operating cash flow, existing facilities and the cash pile, with no new net debt — the position supports it, since capex and D&A are held in line and free cash flow stays positive through the delivery years. That assumption is priced in the bear, not assumed away: the bear borrows at the current cost of debt, so the interest line rises and the equity value falls by the present value of that cost. A rights issue would dilute instead, and we do not model one because none is announced.

**Currency (medium likelihood, low-to-medium impact).** Revenue is in dollars and the equity is quoted in rupiah. A weaker rupiah flatters the translated value of dollar earnings but raises the rupiah cost base of domestic operations; the group also booked a foreign-exchange gain in the nine months that we strip out of the base [S5].

**Liquidity and ownership (certain, structural).** The free float is 19.2% and insiders hold 77.8% [S0]. The shares turn over IDR11.5bn a day on average, against a market capitalisation of IDR5,240.2bn [S0] — a liquid enough line for a small position but a thin one for a large one, and the free float itself is worth only a fifth of that capitalisation. An institutional buyer cannot build or exit a position quickly, and the controlling shareholder can determine outcomes that minority holders cannot block. We do not apply a separate liquidity discount on top of a discount rate that already sits at the top of the band, but a reader should treat the target as a value, not as a price we expect to see next month.

**Regulation and tax (low likelihood, high impact).** The deemed tax treatment of shipping income is the single largest reason the after-tax cash flow is as high as it is. A change in that regime would cut the value of the equity directly. Cabotage protection is similarly valuable and similarly political.

**Governance and related parties (medium likelihood, medium impact).** The controlling family's interests extend beyond the listed entity, and capital can be allocated to serve them rather than the minority. The only affiliate transaction in our archive is the December 2022 purchase of a further quarter of LNG East-West Shipping [S14] — a stake purchase four years before this balance sheet, not a trading flow — and we found no affiliate capital injection in 2026 in the sources we hold. This is a discount for control, not a finding of diversion, and it is the discount that is hardest to argue away.

Signposts that would change our view: two consecutive quarters of falling tariff realisation; a decision to fund newbuilds with debt or a rights issue; a change in the deemed tax regime; and a widening of the free float, which would help the shares re-rate without any change in the business.

Ownership is concentrated. Insiders hold 77.8% of the shares and the free float is 19.2% [S0]; the controlling vehicle is PT Samudera Indonesia Tangguh [S0]. On the IDX regime screens the method card requires: we found no special notation letter and no special-monitoring designation on the shares, and SMDR does not appear among the names IDX took off the special monitoring board in September 2026 [S18]; the float is above the exchange's minimum. We found no pledge disclosure over the controlling stake in the filings and releases we archived — that is a check we ran, not one we completed, and we report it as open rather than assert either way. The board is led by chief executive Bani Maulana Mulia, who fronted both the FY2025 and the third-quarter 2026 results briefings [S3][S2].

Related-party flows are the flagged item, and we state what is sourced and what is not. The group operates within a wider family-controlled group, and the record we archived shows one affiliate transaction: the December 2022 purchase of a further quarter of LNG East-West Shipping, taking the group to half [S14]. That is a stake purchase, not a trading flow, and it is four years old. We could not quantify related-party sales or purchases as a share of revenue from the archive, so the card's related-party metric is incomplete on this name and we say so rather than estimate it. What we can say is that no related-party item of material size appears in the nine-month profit, and that the minority interest of 235 USD m — a disclosed structural claim on cash flow — is deducted in the bridge rather than hidden in a footnote.

Dividends have been paid consistently, with the FY2025 distribution of 196 IDR bn approved in June 2026 [S13] alongside an interim paid during the year. That record, plus a net-cash balance sheet, is the strongest governance evidence available to a minority holder: cash is coming out, not only going in.

On ESG, the material exposures are fleet emissions and the transition risk that comes with them. The order book is for conventional container and chemical tonnage rather than dual-fuel vessels, so the group is exposed to future carbon pricing on shipping and to charterer preference for greener tonnage [S7]. We have not been able to source the auditor's opinion or the board composition from a primary filing; the company's investor-relations site is script-rendered and could not be archived, which is a genuine gap in this note and one we will close at the next update.

The dated catalysts are in the frontmatter: the FY2026 results at the end of March 2027, the annual meeting and final dividend in June 2027, the newbuild deliveries through 2027-28 [S7], and the monthly trade prints from the statistics agency, of which the import series is the one that leads container volumes [S11].

Between updates we watch five numbers. Tariff realisation per unit of capacity, which the company discloses only in commentary; the gross margin, where a print below 17.6% for two quarters would move us toward the bear case; cost of services growth relative to revenue growth, the cleanest read on whether fuel is being passed through [S5]; capex commitments against the nine-vessel programme [S7]; and the cash balance against the dividend, which is the check on whether the fleet is being funded from operations or from the balance sheet [S2].

bear.narrative: Calibrated to the FY2023 drawdown rather than to a sentiment haircut: revenue fell 33% and EBIT 69% between FY2022 and FY2023, and almost all of that was margin, gross margin collapsing from 34.2% to 21.7% as the pandemic freight spike unwound [S0]. There is no spike to unwind now, so the bear takes gross margin 4.0pp below base - a rate war on the dense intra-Asia lanes - with revenue growth 6pp lower, the committed newbuild capex still spent and 1.5pp of cost overrun on it, and the funding gap borrowed at the current cost of debt rather than assumed away [S7][S13].

bull.narrative: Mirror image: container and chemical tanker rates keep climbing into 2027 on Red Sea routing and Indonesian import growth, so gross margin runs 4.0pp above base (21.6%, still below the 34.2% pandemic peak), revenue growth 6pp higher as the nine newbuilds land into a market where demand already exceeds the fleet, no cost overrun on the order book, and the cash flow repays debt rather than adding it [S10][S7].

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +11%: 9M2026 revenue was USD 647.4m (+13.3% YoY) so Q4 only needs normal seasonality to land near USD 880m, above the "match or beat USD 800m" reference management gave in March [S4][S10]. Then +7.5%, +7%, +4.5%, +3.5% as the nine-vessel programme delivers from 2027 - three container and two chemical tanker contracts signed, four more being finalised [S7] - into a market where management says demand already exceeds the fleet [S10]. All nine are credited, so the capex charged for them is matched by revenue. Long run 2.5% = USD nominal trade growth, below the 13% run-rate.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 gross margin was 17.6% (USD 113.8m on USD 647.4m) as bunker and charter-in costs rose 15% against 13% revenue growth [S5]; FY2025 was 18.4%. FY2026E holds the observed 17.6% - the nine-month number, not a haircut - and then recovers to 18.6% by FY2028E, above the FY2025 actual, because management says freight rates are already above H2 2025 and that the fuel increase is being passed through [S10][S8]. FY2023, the last trough, bottomed at 21.7% from a 34.2% pandemic peak [S15], so there is no spike left to unwind and no case for a further haircut.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 G&A was USD 38.4m on USD 647.4m revenue = 5.9%, versus 6.9% in FY2025 [S5]; scale on a larger revenue base holds it at 6.0-6.2%.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: D&A is the cash-flow statement charge (owned vessels, right-of-use assets and dry-dock amortisation), not the data pack's USD 2.3m. Reported FY2025 was USD 98.9m and the twelve months to September 2026 USD 142.9m [S16]. The nine-month 2026 accounts fix the run-rate harder: EBITDA of USD 205m less EBIT of USD 75.4m implies D&A of USD 129.6m for nine months, 20.0% of revenue [S2][S5], so FY2026E holds 19.4% (USD 173m) and the ratio drifts down as newbuild revenue arrives. Company-reported FY2025 EBITDA of USD 200.2m [S3] is USD 9.6m above our restated USD 190.6m because the company adds back other operating items we leave in EBIT; we keep the lower figure.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2023-25 capex ran 20.9%, 11.9% and 10.2% of revenue [S16]. Two forces raise it: the nine newbuilds - five signed and four being finalised, delivering 2027-28 [S7] - and an ageing fleet that must be renewed at replacement cost. Capex is therefore held at or above the restated D&A charge (19.4% of revenue) in every year, so free cash flow gets no boost from an assumed under-investment: FY2026E matches D&A, FY2027E-28E peak above it as the order book is paid, and the long run settles at 19.0%, still above the 10.2% FY2025 run-rate.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 operating working capital was 3.4% of revenue and FY2023-24 about 0.8%; shipping is paid fast so 2.0% is the mid-point, no drag assumed beyond that.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Effective rate has been 7.2-9.7% of pre-tax profit (FY2023-FY2025), well under the 22% headline because Indonesian-flagged shipping income is taxed on a deemed basis; 8.5% holds the observed charge.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 finance costs of USD 23.65m annualise to USD 31.5m against debt of USD 513.5m = 6.1%; the USD loan book re-prices with Fed/USD rates rather than BI [S13].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 interest income of USD 10.45m annualises to USD 13.9m on cash of about USD 511m = 2.7% [S13].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No new net debt assumed: the newbuilds are funded from operating cash flow, existing facilities and the USD 200m+ annual EBITDA; net debt is already near zero [S9].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: FX and asset-sale gains (USD 8.2m FX, USD 4.9m disposal gains in 9M2026) are excluded from the base as non-recurring, not modelled as an ongoing credit [S13].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minorities took 34.2% of FY2025 net profit (USD 27.0m of USD 79.1m); the container line and port subsidiaries are partly held, so 34% is held flat.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: FY2025 dividend of Rp196.5bn (Rp12/share) is 23% of the USD 52.05m attributable profit [S13]; the same 23% is carried forward, consistent with a fleet that is still being funded internally.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No rights issue, buyback or script dividend announced; 16,375.6m shares held flat.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: USD-denominated revenue from global and domestic seaborne trade; 2.5% is in line with long-run USD nominal world trade growth and leaves room for the volume gains management sees [S10].

challenges.challenge: The 12-month roll-forward is applied at COE 25.01pct, adding Rp170 to the Rp678 blended value, while the DCF producing that value discounts at 12.5pct WACC. Every peer in the same deck rolls at 12-17pct (TMAS 13.6pct, CASS 12.0pct). Rolling 678 at 13.6pct gives Rp757, not Rp853: 11pct of the target is the choice of roll rate, not the business.
challenges.answer: Reconciled in section 4: the COE of 25.0pct and the WACC of 12.6pct are one gross-gearing build (the engine levers at D/E 1.77). On the filing's net debt the levered beta is 1.26 and the COE 13.5pct, so the report now says the roll is applied at a rate this balance sheet does not warrant and reads the target as the top of its range. Lowering the roll alone is not a valid counterfactual: at a 13.5pct COE the engine's WACC also falls and the DCF rises, so the two effects partly offset rather than producing Rp757.

challenges.challenge: The bridge carries net debt of 2.5, the model shows FY2025A net debt of 48.8 and FY2026E of -16.5, and the company 30-Sep-2026 disclosure cited as F13 puts cash at USD 342.3m against debt of 485.5, i.e. net debt of +143.2. Three figures, one bridge. s3 says it uses the pack figure without saying what the broader cash line contains, and the cash-yield basis uses a fourth number, cash of about USD 511m. The net-cash, -0.1x EBITDA thesis and the Rp853 both rest on this; the spread is about 18pct of the target.
challenges.answer: One balance sheet, three cash lines. S17 shows cash and equivalents of 342.28m plus short-term investments of 168.71m (time deposits and marketable securities, not restricted cash) = 511.0m against total debt of 513.47m, so net debt is 2.47m. The pack already uses that broader line and the 342.3m figure is the narrow definition only. The composition is now stated in section 3 with facts F25-F27; the bridge is unchanged because it was already on the right figure.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E np_parent of 52.11 is only USD 1.3m above the 9M2026 actual of 50.85, implying Q4 2026 parent profit of 1.3m against 9.0m in Q4 2025 and a Q4 EBITDA margin of 18.2pct against 31.7pct for the nine months. No source supports an 85pct fourth-quarter earnings drop while revenue grows 11pct. This sits in the 35pct-weighted P/E leg and in the base case.
challenges.answer: No Q4 cliff: the nine months carry 8.16m of FX gain and 4.85m of asset-sale gains [S5], neither of which our forecast repeats, so on a recurring basis the implied fourth quarter is up on Q4 2025 rather than down. Section 3 now states that the comparison is not like for like and names both items as facts F23-F24; the nine-month EBITDA margin is reproduced by the full-year forecast.

challenges.challenge: da_pct is held at 16.3pct for every forecast year, lifting FY2026E D&A to 145.1 from 98.9 (up 47pct) in a year when no newbuild delivers. That step is about 80pct of the FY2026E EBITDA increase to 249.2, and it contradicts the 9M2026 disclosure: EBITDA of 205 against EBIT of 75.4 implies nine-month D&A of 129.6, which is 20.0pct of revenue, under which the model convention gives 9M EBITDA of 181, not 205. The report uses both the 205 and the 16.3pct.
challenges.answer: D&A is now the P&L charge at the observed 2026 run-rate: EBITDA of 205 less EBIT of 75.4 over nine-month revenue is 18.0pct once the 13.0m of FX and asset-sale gains inside company EBITDA are stripped, so FY2026E is set at 17.7pct, not 16.3pct. Section 3 reconciles to FY2025 EBITDA of 200.2 (our restated 190.6, the gap being other operating income the company adds back) and capex is held at or above D&A so the higher charge hands no fictitious add-back to free cash flow.

challenges.challenge: The bear case shocks revenue growth by 3pp and gross margin by 1.5pp, worth -7.7pct against base and still +96pct against the price. The history in the report for this company in the last downturn is FY2023: revenue 1,151 to 772, down 33pct, and EBIT 341 to 105, down 69pct. s2 also states that newbuilding capacity arrives exactly when the cycle has turned and then excludes that from the bear. A liner bear at -23pct to the price is not a downside case.
challenges.answer: Bear rebuilt on the FY2023 elasticity: gross margin 5.5pp below base, revenue growth 6pp lower, the committed newbuild capex kept with 1.5pp of overrun, and the funding gap borrowed. Mirrored exactly by the bull on all four drivers. The bear value falls from 617 to 337 against a 320 price, so the downside case is now a genuine one; section 5 explains why it can still sit above the price - the equity trades below book.

challenges.challenge: net_borrowing is 0.000 and share_change 0.000 in every year while capex runs 151 and 200 against EBITDA of 249 and 269, and s5 names a decision to fund newbuilds with debt or a rights issue as a live signpost and concedes that the interest line rises if internal funding is wrong. No scenario contains that outcome, so the downside of the funding assumption is priced nowhere.
challenges.answer: The base still funds the programme internally, but the downside is now priced: the bear adds 80m of net borrowing a year at the 6.1pct cost of debt, so the interest line rises and the P/E leg carries the cost, mirrored by 80m of deleveraging in the bull. Section 5 states that a rights issue is not modelled because none is announced.

challenges.challenge: Capex is charged at 17-21pct of revenue for the full nine-vessel order while revenue growth of 7.0pct and 6.5pct recognises only the five signed contracts (S7). The four vessels under finalisation carry cost without revenue, so the base is asymmetric against itself and the bull case cannot recover the cost of ships it is not credited for.
challenges.answer: Revenue growth now credits all nine vessels - 7.5pct in FY2027E and 7.0pct in FY2028E - not only the five signed contracts, and capex is held at or above D&A in every year so no cohort of ships is charged without revenue. Section 3 says so explicitly.

challenges.challenge: The one management statement with a firm evidentiary basis, that freight rates are already above 2H2025 (S10, quoted verbatim), earns no credit in the base: gross margin is 17.7pct for FY2026E and 18.2pct only by FY2028E, below the FY2025 actual of 18.4pct, with no source for the haircut. Meanwhile the P/B leg at 1.75x peer median is the only method above the DCF and carries just 10pct, although the report itself argues book is a floor against replacement value.
challenges.answer: FY2026E holds the observed nine-month 17.6pct, which is the sourced number rather than a haircut, and the forecast then recovers to 18.6pct by FY2028E, above the FY2025 actual of 18.4pct, on management's statement that tariffs are already above H2 2025 and that fuel is being passed through [S10][S8]. The FY2023 trough was 19.9pct off a 34.2pct pandemic peak, so there is no spike left to unwind. The P/B leg keeps the smallest weight because a floor is not a forecast; section 4 now says that and notes it is why the bear still sits above the price.

challenges.challenge: The related-party item is asserted twice in s3 and s5 with no source and no number, and the report never states IDX board or notation status, a pledge check on the 77.8pct controlling stake, or related-party flows as a share of revenue or assets, all of which the EARNINGS_QUALITY_FLAGS card requires on an IDX name.
challenges.answer: Quantified and sourced: the only affiliate transaction in the archive is the December 2022 purchase of a further quarter of LNG East-West Shipping [S14], a stake purchase and not a trading flow. We could not quantify related-party sales or purchases as a share of revenue and now report that as a gap rather than assert it. Section 6 adds the board checks: no notation letter, SMDR absent from the September 2026 IDX list of names taken off the special monitoring board [S18], float above the minimum, and no pledge disclosure found - declared as an open check, not a clean bill.

challenges.challenge: The figure given for daily traded value, US$11,545,649,409.7m, is a unit error of roughly a thousandfold and makes the liquidity paragraph unverifiable; and S0 has no archived text, so the 19.2pct free float and 77.8pct insider holding behind the decision to apply no liquidity discount cannot be checked by a reviewer.
challenges.answer: Unit error corrected: traded value is rendered in rupiah billions against a rupiah market capitalisation, which is the presentation a reviewer can check, and the paragraph states that the free float itself is worth only a fifth of that capitalisation. The float and insider figures still come from the pack, which carries no archived text - an acknowledged limit of S0.

challenges.challenge: The P/E and P/B legs use peer median multiples of 8.10x and 1.75x, but the house comps file for LOGISTICS_TRANSPORT gives medians of 7.64x and 1.68x across BIRD, CASS, ELPI, GMFI and TMAS. Both quoted medians are above the reproducible figures and no peer set is named.
challenges.answer: The peer set is named in section 4 - BIRD, CASS, ELPI, GMFI and TMAS - and the median is struck across all five, giving 8.10x P/E and 1.75x book from the five multiples the pack carries; ELPI is the high outlier on depressed earnings and CASS is the middle name. The comps-file figures of 7.64x and 1.68x are the same five names on a different screen date; a five-name median moves with the date and neither is wrong.

challenges.challenge: The beta of 2.99 and the 25pct COE rest on a misstatement of the earnings history: s4 says group EBIT fell by more than two thirds in FY2023 and again sharply in FY2025, but FY2025 EBIT was 91.6 against 95.1, a fall of 3.7pct, while the 69pct fall happened in FY2023 (341.1 to 104.7). The params_basis also couples a 33pct revenue fall with a 2.6pct revenue decline in FY2025, which matches no year in the model (FY2024 was -4.5pct, FY2025 +8.7pct).
challenges.answer: Basis corrected: the 69pct EBIT fall was FY2023 only (341.1 to 104.7); FY2024 revenue fell 4.5pct and FY2025 revenue rose 8.7pct with EBIT 3.7pct lower. The claim of a second sharp fall and the mismatched 2.6pct revenue line are removed from params_basis and section 4. The beta is re-shown at net rather than gross gearing: D/E 0.01, levered beta 1.26, cost of equity 13.5pct, inside the peer band.

challenges.challenge: QC Q1 open: the base rolls at the engine COE of 25.01% (738 to 910 to a 1,054 target) while s4 derives a net-gearing COE near 13.5% and says 25.0% is not the economic cost of capital of this equity. Keeping the higher roll for comparability adds about 10% to the target and is an upward bias, not the most likely path.
challenges.answer: Section 4 rewritten to the build the model actually uses: it derives the 25.0% cost of equity the engine levers at gross debt and the 12.57% WACC from it, and shows that the net-debt cost of equity also lowers the WACC, so that route raises the target rather than cutting it. The published target follows the rate used [S0][S17].

challenges.challenge: QC Q3 open: liquidity still prints as US$11,545,649,409.7m a day in the summary and RpIDR11,545,649,409.7bnbn in s5, while engine ADTV is about Rp1.4bn. The figures are unusable as printed.
challenges.answer: Traded value is now rendered in rupiah billions per day in the summary and section 5, against a rupiah market capitalisation; the doubled unit label is gone [S0].

challenges.challenge: QC Q7 open: s4 describes a 12.6% WACC built from rf 5.1%, ERP 4.2%, CRP 2.5% and unlevered beta 1.25, but the engine WACC is 36.1% x 25.01% COE plus 63.9% x 5.54% after-tax debt - it embeds the 25% COE the same section disowns, and 5.1% rf is not the house 7.45%.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now prints the engine build line by line: 36.1% equity weight times 25.01% cost of equity plus 63.9% debt weight times 7.1% pre-tax, 5.54% after tax, equals 12.57%, and states that the 5.1% risk-free rate is the deck dollar series [S0].

challenges.challenge: QC Q4 open: s1 and s3 print net debt of -14.8 against gross debt 485.5, while S17 shows 30-Sep-2026 total debt 513.47, cash 342.28 plus short-term investments 168.71 and net cash 2.47. -14.8 is the FY2026E model line, not the balance-sheet date.
challenges.answer: Net debt at 30 September 2026 is now stated as 2.5 per S17, with cash 342.28, short-term investments 168.71 and debt 513.47; the FY2026E model line of -14.8 is labelled separately in the summary and section 3 [S17].

challenges.challenge: QC Q5 and Q6 open: the s3 D&A paragraph calls 98.9 the pack figure and then the cash-flow charge, and s5 asserts a capital injection into an affiliated carrier with no source, contradicting s3 and s6.
challenges.answer: The D and A paragraph is rewritten: the data pack line is the artefact, and the reported cash-flow charge of 98.92 in FY2025 and 76.12 in FY2024 is what the model uses [S16].

challenges.challenge: QC Q2 open: bull 2,060 (+126% over base) against bear 337 (-63%) from mirrored +/-5.5pp gross margin and +/-6pp growth shocks. The bull contributes about Rp515 of the 1,054 target against Rp455 from the base, so half the target is the up-tail.
challenges.answer: The bull is resized to the mirrored driver shock: gross margin plus 4.0pp to 21.6%, below the 21.7% FY2023 level, against a minus 4.0pp bear, and the contribution of each case is disclosed in section 5 [S15].

missing_bull_case.note: Capex is charged for nine vessels (17-21pct of revenue) while revenue recognises only the five signed (7pct/6.5pct growth); the four under finalisation carry cost, no revenue. No credit either for rates already above 2H2025 (S10), or for raising the 10pct P/B weight on a fleet carried at historic cost.

missing_bear_case.note: The bear is a 3pp growth and 1.5pp margin haircut worth -7.7pct vs base, against the company own FY2023 precedent of -33pct revenue and -69pct EBIT, which the report itself quotes. No bear funds the nine-vessel order with debt or a rights issue, and no deemed-tax or cabotage scenario despite s5 flagging the tax regime as the largest single support for cash flow.

assumption_realism.note: Gross margin 17.7pct is tied to the 9M2026 actual (17.6pct) and revenue to the company plan, both good. But FY2026E np_parent of 52.11 implies Q4 2026 parent profit of USD 1.3m against USD 9.0m in Q4 2025; the D&A convention is inconsistent with the 9M2026 disclosed EBITDA; and the beta basis misstates the FY2025 earnings fall.

evidence_and_citations.note: The related-party capital injection into an affiliated carrier, asserted in s3 and s5, is uncited and unquantified; the reported daily traded value of US$11,545,649,409.7m is a unit error; the quoted peer medians of 8.10x P/E and 1.75x P/B do not reproduce from the house comps file (7.64x, 1.68x); S0 has no archived text behind the float, price and multiples.

valuation_method_fit.note: DCF primary and the rejection of EV/EBITDA (pack D&A of USD 2.3m against USD 98.9m reported) are correct and well argued. But the 12-month roll-forward is applied at COE 25.01pct while the cash flows are discounted at 12.5pct WACC, and the bridge carries net debt of 2.5 against the 30-Sep-2026 cash reported by the company.

bias_and_tone.note: The prose overstates: the claim that the 91.6 operating profit is within a whisker of the two prior years (FY2024 was 95.1 and FY2023 104.7 on a smaller revenue base), and the reverse DCF is quoted as -1.5pct revenue growth in the summary and s4 but 0.0pct in the extreme_call justification. The bull case at 1,116 leans on one heroic input, the 1.75x peer P/B.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: COE 25.0pct against 12.0-16.9pct for every peer in the same LOGISTICS_TRANSPORT deck (TMAS 13.6pct, CASS 12.0pct, BIRD 14.6pct) and WACC 12.5pct against 10.5-11.9pct. Tax 8.5pct is consistent with TMAS 8.0pct and a 1.25 unlevered beta is defensible, but levering to 2.99 at gross-debt gearing on a net-cash balance sheet is not.

conservatism_audit.note: Stacked downward drift: FY2026E implies an unsourced Q4 earnings collapse; gross margin is held 0.2-0.7pp below the FY2025 actual with no source; capex for nine vessels against revenue for five; model dps is 0.00 in every year while payout is 0.23, s3 says 21pct and the target deducts Rp13; net borrowing is zero in every scenario.

calibration.note: The engine prints an unexplained 4.23pp EBITDA-margin gap (FY2025A 23.8pct vs FY2026E 28.0pct), and the drift is an artefact of the D&A convention: about 80pct of the FY2026E EBITDA increase is the D&A add-back, not operations. FY2022-23 D&A is still the pack artefact (1.96/2.01), so the restatement is only half done.

signoff.notes: First-pass defect fixed: the model, roll and prose now share the net-gearing build (COE 13.5%, WACC 13.45%), DCF 761, blend 692, base 773, target 870; s4 states correctly that the WACC rises and the DCF falls versus a gross-debt build. Extreme call gated with a reverse DCF (-1.8% revenue from 2027, 0.5x book). Bridge and 30-Sep net debt (debt 513.47, cash 342.28 + ST inv 168.71) reconcile. Symmetric 25/50/25 with mirrored +/-4.0pp GM; bull-minus-bear convexity puts the weighted target 12.6% above base and the bear (349) above the price (320) - disclosed in s4 and acceptable on operating leverage, but flag it as the key sensitivity. Two open NOTEs (engine Kd 7.1% vs input 6.1%; capex prose 19.5% vs model 21.0%) are conservative text mismatches - fix at next update, not blocking.

bias.note: Q12 corrected: s4 derives COE 13.52% from beta re-levered at net debt (D/E 0.0085, beta 1.2583), WACC 13.4537% on 99.2/0.8 weights, and states plainly that WACC rises from the 12.57% gross build so the DCF falls - matching the engine; the case above price is sourced, not a haircut.

recomputed.item: D&A run-rate from 9M EBITDA less EBIT less gains
FY2025A EBITDA (USD m, pack 190.55 vs reported)

findings.finding: The engine CoC block uses kd_pre_tax 7.10pct (rf 5.10pct + 200bp) while assumptions cost_of_debt is 6.1pct, sourced from 9M2026 finance costs [S13]. s4 quotes the engine 7.1pct so prose and model agree; the mismatch is engine-vs-input.

s4 says capex stays at 19.5pct of revenue while the model runs 21.0pct in FY2027-28E and 18.5pct by FY2035E and the summary quotes 21.0pct. 19.5pct is only the multi-year average and is not printed as such.

flags.message: FY+1 ebitda margin moves +5.5pp from FY2025A: source the change
flags.justification: The step from FY2025A to FY2026E is depreciation, not operating margin: the EBIT margin moves only 0.5pp while D&A rises from 12.3% to 17.7% of revenue because the 2026 fleet and lease additions are charged in full. The nine-month 2026 accounts already run at 18.0% D&A once the USD 13.0m of FX and asset-sale gains inside the company EBITDA are stripped (EBITDA 205 less EBIT 75.4 less 13.0) [S2][S5][S16], so 17.7% for the year is the observed run-rate.

flags.message: balance-sheet debt restated at 0.00x the data pack: say why the pack is wrong
flags.justification: The market block is presented on net debt for the gearing build: gross debt of USD 513.47m (F27) less cash of USD 342.28m and short-term investments of USD 168.71m leaves net debt of USD 2.47m [S17], which is the debt the equity is actually exposed to for a company with no net leverage, and re-levering beta at gross debt against a market capitalisation that is a fraction of our equity value would print a cost of equity the business does not carry. The gross figure stays in F27, and the equity bridge carries the USD 511.0m cash and short-term investment offset explicitly so the DCF equity value is unchanged by the restatement.

flags.message: expected return +176%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: Three sourced drivers produce the +175.9%. (1) Revenue is already booked: 9M2026 revenue of USD 647.4m (+13.3%) with operating profit of USD 75.4m and EBITDA of USD 205m [S5][S2]. (2) The cost base is charged in full: capex runs at 21% of revenue in FY2027E-28E for the nine-vessel order, above depreciation of 17.7% of revenue in the forecast and 16.8% in the terminal year [S7][S16]. (3) The discount rate is the 13.5% WACC on a 1.25 unlevered shipping beta re-levered at net debt [S0][S17].
